title: Sialic acid exacerbates polycystic ovary syndrome in mice by modulating gut microbiota-mediated bile acid metabolism and FXR activation

paper_content.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent endocrine disorder in women. Accumulating evidence indicates that gut dysbiosis and metabolic disturbances are associated with the pathogenesis of PCOS. However, the mechanisms by which metabolic alterations influence gut homeostasis and contribute to PCOS progression remain poorly understood. Here, we show that N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) exacerbates dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)-induced PCOS phenotypes in female mice in a gut microbiota-dependent manner. Specifically, Neu5Ac promotes the expansion of the gut Ligilactobacillus salivarius (L. sa) with bile salt hydrolase (BSH) activity. Administration of L. sa to DHEA-treated mice worsens PCOS symptoms by reducing levels of the conjugated bile acid tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) via BSH activity. Reduced TUDCA enhances intestinal farnesoid X receptor (FXR) activation, leading to suppression of IL-22 production. Mechanistically, IL-22 attenuates DHEA-induced ovarian ferroptosis by activating the STAT3 signaling pathway. These findings reveal that sialic acid-mediated bile acid–FXR–IL-22 signaling contributes to PCOS pathogenesis, highlighting a potential therapeutic strategy for PCOS intervention.
paper_content.introduction:
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent endocrine disorder characterized by ovarian dysfunction and insulin resistance, adversely affecting ovarian health and female reproductive function 1,2. In PCOS, the ovary exhibits increased inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death, including ferroptosis 3-5. Deficiency of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a key regulator of redox homeostasis during ferroptosis, exacerbates ferroptosis and contributes to endometrial epithelial fibrosis in PCOS 5. Additionally, the gut microbiota has been implicated in PCOS pathogenesis 6-8. For instance, patients with PCOS exhibit significant gut dysbiosis, particularly elevated levels of fecal Bacteroides vulgatus (B. vulgatus), and administration of B. vulgatus induces PCOS-like symptoms in mice 1,7. Modulation of the gut microbiota through inulin and tempol treatment alleviates PCOS and associated metabolic disturbances 9,10. However, the roles of specific microbial species in PCOS pathogenesis remains poorly understood.

Gut microbiota-derived metabolites are key mediators that regulate the crosstalk between the intestinal microbiota and the host. For example, patients with PCOS exhibit altered bile acid profiles, particularly increased levels of non-conjugated bile acids and reduced levels of conjugated bile acids such as glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCA) and tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) 1. Treatment of mice with GDCA and TUDCA ameliorates PCOS by increasing interleukin-22 (IL-22) levels 1, which may be attributed to enhanced IL-22 production and subsequent activation of signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) 1,11. Conjugated bile acids can be converted into non-conjugated forms by gut microbiota through bile salt hydrolase (BSH) activity 12, and bacterial genera enriched in PCOS patients—such as Bacteroides and Lactobacillus—exhibit high BSH expression 13,14. Notably, conjugated bile acids, including TUDCA, and GDCA, typically act as antagonists of farnesoid X receptor (FXR) 12,14-16. Enhanced intestinal FXR activation promotes the development of metabolic disorders through multiple mechanisms, such as promoting ceramide synthesis 17. Additionally, gut-specific FXR activation reduces IL-22 levels by promoting intestinal epithelial ferroptosis and lipid peroxide accumulation 18. Inhibition of BSH activity or intestinal FXR signaling exerts beneficial effects against metabolic syndrome and pathological cell death 18,19.

Although gut microbiota-derived metabolites directly influence metabolic health and the development of PCOS—such as agmatine produced by B. vulgatus, which promotes PCOS via FXR activation 7, and AT-C1, a metabolite derived from Aspergillus tubingensis, which induces PCOS by suppressing IL-22 production 8—the reciprocal impact of microbial metabolism on gut homeostasis remains poorly understood. For example, alterations in the gut microbiota and the presence of gut inflammation increase the release of free N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac, also known as sialic acid), a 9-carbon monosaccharide located on the outer layer of the intestinal mucosa 20. This release exacerbates gut dysbiosis, promotes intestinal inflammation, and contributes to extraintestinal diseases such as mastitis 20-23. Bacteroides efficiently produces free sialic acid via its sialidase enzyme but lacks the capacity to utilize sialic acid for growth 20. In contrast, commensal Lactobacillus and opportunistic pathobionts such as Escherichia/Shigella can exploit sialic acid as a carbon source to support their proliferation in the gut, thereby influencing disease outcomes 21. However, it remains unclear whether Bacteroides-derived sialic acid facilitates the expansion of Lactobacillus and Escherichia/Shigella and thereby promotes the development of PCOS.

In this study, we found that patients with PCOS exhibited elevated fecal Neu5Ac levels, which exacerbated PCOS in a gut microbiota-dependent manner. Specifically, Neu5Ac treatment promoted the expansion of the gut Ligilactobacillus salivarius (L. sa) and increased BSH activity, thereby reducing levels of the conjugated bile acid TUDCA, enhancing intestinal FXR activation, and suppressing IL-22 release. This cascade ultimately aggravates PCOS by promoting ovarian ferroptosis through modulation of STAT3 signaling. These findings indicate that sialic acid promotes gut dysbiosis and FXR activation, thereby exacerbating PCOS outcomes.
paper_content.results:
1. Neu5Ac exacerbate DHEA-induced PCOS in mice in a gut microbiota-dependent manner.
To investigate metabolic alterations associated with PCOS, fecal samples were collected from 16 PCOS patients (P) and 16 controls (C) for untargeted metabolomics analysis (clinical characteristics are provided in Supplementary Table 1). Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed a clear separation between the metabolic profiles of PCOS patients and control individuals (Fig. 1A). This distinction was further confirmed by partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) score plots (Fig. S1A). Additionally, volcano plots illustrated the global distribution of differentially expressed metabolites (Fig. 1B). Compared with the control group, 332 upregulated and 274 downregulated metabolites were identified in PCOS patients (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Data 1). Notably, among the 20 most abundant metabolites, Neu5Ac was significantly increased in the P group and exhibited the lowest p-value (Fig. 1C). We further confirmed that PCOS patients had higher fecal Neu5Ac levels than those in the C group (Fig. 1D). This finding was replicated in an independent cohort consisting of 19 PCOS patients and 14 control individuals (Fig. 1E and Supplementary Table 2). However, no significant difference in Neu5Ac levels was observed in serum between PCOS patients and controls (Fig. S1B). Moreover, fecal Neu5Ac, but not serum levels, showed a positive correlation with PCOS severity and insulin resistance (Fig. 1F).

Similarly, mice subjected to DHEA treatment exhibited increased fecal Neu5Ac levels compared to the control group (Fig. 1G). Neu5Ac can be produced by both microbial and host cells, and elevated free Neu5Ac has been closely linked to inflammation and disease progression 21,22. We then investigated whether exogenous Neu5Ac administration influences DHEA-induced PCOS in mice (Fig. 1H). The results showed that Neu5Ac administration exacerbated insulin resistance induced by DHEA, as assessed by glucose tolerance tests (GTTs) and insulin tolerance tests (ITTs) (Fig. 1I and S1C). Moreover, Neu5Ac treatment aggravated DHEA-induced disruptions in the estrous cycle (Fig. 1J and S1D). Histological analysis demonstrated that DHEA-treated mice displayed ovarian morphological impairments, characterized by an increased number of cyst-like follicles and a reduced number of corpora lutea compared to controls; these abnormalities were further exacerbated by Neu5Ac administration (Fig. 1K, S1E and F). Consistently, Neu5Ac treatment enhanced the DHEA-induced increases in serum hormone levels, including testosterone and luteinizing hormone (LH) (Fig. S1G).

Since sialic acids, including Neu5Ac, have been reported to modulate the gut microbiota and promote inflammatory responses 21,22, we further investigated whether the effects of Neu5Ac on PCOS are mediated by the gut microbiota. First, mice were pretreated with antibiotics (ABX) to deplete commensal microbes prior to administration of Neu5Ac and DHEA (Fig. S1H). The results showed that ABX treatment abolished the exacerbating effect of Neu5Ac on DHEA-induced insulin resistance (Fig. S1I and J). ABX administration also reversed the aggravation of Neu5Ac on DHEA-induced disruptions in the estrous cycle (Fig. S1K and L). Moreover, depletion of the gut microbiota eliminated the worsening effects of Neu5Ac on ovarian histological alterations under DHEA treatment (Fig. S1M), as well as on elevated serum testosterone and LH levels (Fig. S1N). To confirm these findings, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) was performed using donor mice treated with Neu5Ac (N-FMT) or vehicle control (C-FMT) (Fig. 1L). We found that mice receiving N-FMT exhibited lower insulin sensitivity than those receiving C-FMT following DHEA treatment (Fig. 1M and S2A). N-FMT also exacerbated DHEA-induced estrous cycle disruptions (Fig. 1N and S2B). Additionally, mice receiving N-FMT displayed more severe ovarian histological damage compared to those receiving C-FMT (Fig. 1O and P), along with higher serum testosterone and LH levels (Fig. S2C). Altogether, these results demonstrate that Neu5Ac exacerbates DHEA-induced PCOS in a gut microbiota-dependent manner.

2. Neu5Ac exacerbates DHEA-induced PCOS by promoting Ligilactobacillus expansion.
We next investigated how Neu5Ac treatment alters the gut microbiota in the context of DHEA-induced PCOS. The results showed that Neu5Ac treatment induced only minor changes in the alpha diversity of the gut microbiota (Fig. 2A and S2D). However, Neu5Ac significantly altered gut microbial community structure (Fig. 2B). At the phylum level, increased abundances of Bacillota and Campylobacterota, and reduced abundance of Bacteroidota were observed in DHEA-treated mice compared to the control group (Fig. 2C). Notably, these alterations were further enhanced by Neu5Ac treatment (Fig. 2C). At the genus level, Neu5Ac promoted the expansion of Ligilactobacillus induced by DHEA (Fig. 2D). Similarly, in recipient mice, no significant differences were detected in alpha diversity indices between N-FMT and C-FMT groups (Fig. S2E). Consistently, N-FMT significantly altered gut microbial structures compared to C-FMT (Fig. 2E). At the phylum level, N-FMT increased Bacillota and Campylobacterota abundances and decreased Bacteroidota abundance relative to C-FMT (Fig. S2F). At the genus level, higher fecal abundances of Ligilactobacillus and Helicobacter were observed in the N-FMT group than the C-FMT group (Fig. 2F). LEfSe analysis further revealed that Ligilactobacillus was enriched in the DHEA group, with greater enrichment following Neu5Ac or N-FMT treatment (Fig. 2G–J), and Neu5Ac treatment alone also increased fecal Ligilactobacillus abundance compared to control mice (Fig. S2G).

We then sought to explore whether the enhanced expansion of Ligilactobacillus contributes to Neu5Ac-mediated exacerbation of DHEA-induced PCOS in mice. First, mice were treated with ampicillin (Amp) or vancomycin (Van) under DHEA and Neu5Ac co-treatment conditions (Fig. 3A), given that Ligilactobacillus is sensitive to ampicillin but resistant to vancomycin 11. Interestingly, Amp treatment, but not Van, alleviated insulin resistance compared to Neu5Ac- and DHEA-treated mice (Fig. 3B and S3A). Improved estrous cyclicity was also observed in Amp-treated mice, but not in Van-treated mice, compared to those receiving both Neu5Ac and DHEA (Fig. 3C and S3B). Moreover, Amp treatment attenuated Neu5Ac-aggravated ovarian damage and serum hormone dysregulation caused by DHEA (Fig. 3D, S3C and D). We next quantified different Ligilactobacillus species using qPCR and found that Ligilactobacillus salivarius (L. sa) was elevated in Neu5Ac+DHEA-exposed mice and N-FMT-treated mice (Fig. 3E and F). Moreover, L. reuteri and L. rhamnosus appeared to be increased in Neu5Ac+DHEA- and N-FMT-treated mice (Fig. S3E and F). However, only L. sa abundance was significantly increased in PCOS patients compared with the control group (Fig. 3G and S3G). Importantly, fecal Neu5Ac levels were positively correlated with L. sa abundance in PCOS patients (Fig. 3H). We then administered L. sa to mice with DHEA-induced PCOS (Fig. 3I). As expected, L. sa treatment exacerbated DHEA-induced insulin resistance and estrous cycle disruption (Fig. 3J–L and S3H). Additionally, L. sa treatment worsened DHEA-induced ovarian injury and increases in serum testosterone and LH levels (Fig. 3M, N and S3I). Since Neu5Ac can promote the growth of both commensal and opportunistic bacteria 21, we cultured L. sa with Neu5Ac and found that Neu5Ac significantly enhanced L. sa growth compared to glucose (Fig. 3O). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Neu5Ac exacerbates DHEA-induced PCOS by promoting Ligilactobacillus expansion.

3. Ligilactobacillus promotes PCOS by altering bile acid profiles via bile salt hydrolase.
Bile acid metabolism is closely associated with the pathogenesis of PCOS 1, and Ligilactobacillus is a key modulator of host bile acid profiles through BSH activity 13,19. We therefore investigated whether bile acid metabolism contributes to Neu5Ac- and L. sa-mediated exacerbation of PCOS. The results showed that DHEA treatment increased levels of unconjugated bile acids and decreased conjugated bile acid levels compared to control mice, and both Neu5Ac and L. sa treatments amplified these effects (Fig. 4A, B, S4A and B). Specifically, Neu5Ac and L. sa appear to facilitate the DHEA-induced reduction in taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) and TUDCA (Fig. 4A, B, S4A and B). In PCOS patients, reduced levels of conjugated bile acids and TUDCA were also detected (Fig. 4C-D). Similarly, DHEA-treated mice exhibited elevated fecal BSH activity, which was further increased by Neu5Ac and L. sa treatments (Fig. 4E and F). Patients with PCOS also exhibited increased BSH activity (Fig. 4G). Moreover, TUDCA levels were negatively correlated with fecal Neu5Ac and L. sa abundance in PCOS patients (Fig. 4H).

To examine the role of conjugated bile acids in Neu5Ac-mediated PCOS exacerbation, we supplemented mice with TUDCA (Fig. 4I). TUDCA administration alleviated insulin resistance induced by combined Neu5Ac and DHEA treatment (Fig. 4J and S4C). Mice receiving TUDCA also showed improved estrous cyclicity compared to those treated with Neu5Ac and DHEA alone (Fig. S4D and E). Moreover, TUDCA treatment attenuated ovarian damage and suppressed the rise in serum hormone levels caused by Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment (Fig. 4K, L and S4F). To confirm the involvement of BSH in mediating unconjugated bile acid production and PCOS exacerbation under Neu5Ac exposure, mice were treated with the BSH inhibitor caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE) 24 (Fig. 4M). Notably, CAPE administration alleviated insulin resistance in Neu5Ac- and DHEA-co-treated mice (Fig. 4N and S4G). Furthermore, CAPE-treated mice exhibited improved estrous cycle regularity compared to the Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment group (Fig. S4H). Additionally, BSH inhibition by CAPE reduced ovarian injury and lowered serum hormone levels in mice exposed to Neu5Ac and DHEA (Fig. 4O, P and S4I). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Neu5Ac-driven Ligilactobacillus expansion promotes PCOS by modulating bile acid metabolism through BSH-mediated deconjugation.

4. Alterations in bile acid profiles exacerbate PCOS by activating FXR.
Since unconjugated bile acids act as FXR ligands and FXR is implicated in the pathogenesis of PCOS 7,16, we investigated whether Neu5Ac- and L. sa-mediated exacerbation of PCOS is regulated by FXR signaling. As expected, DHEA-treated mice exhibited increased Fxr and downstream fibroblast growth factor 15 (Fgf15) mRNA levels in the ileum compared to control mice, and Neu5Ac treatment further enhanced these upregulations (Fig. 5A). Consistently, Neu5Ac exacerbated the DHEA-induced increase in plasma FGF15 concentrations (Fig. 5B). Similar results were observed in L. sa-treated mice (Fig. 5C and D). We confirmed that these changes in FXR and FGF15 were mediated by BSH-derived unconjugated bile acids, as treatment with TUDCA or the BSH inhibitor CAPE suppressed the increases in ileal Fxr and Fgf15 expression and plasma FGF15 levels (Fig. S5A and B). Similarly, patients with PCOS had significantly higher plasma FGF19 levels—a human ortholog of murine FGF15 and a direct FXR target 18, —compared to the control group (Fig. 5E).

To assess the functional role of FXR, mice were treated with the FXR antagonist Gly-β-MCA 18 (Fig. 5F). Gly-β-MCA administration alleviated insulin resistance induced by co-treatment with Neu5Ac and DHEA (Fig. 5G and S5C). Furthermore, Gly-β-MCA improved estrous cycle disruption caused by Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment (Fig. S5D). In addition, FXR inhibition by Gly-β-MCA attenuated ovarian damage and reduced the elevation in serum hormone levels induced by Neu5Ac and DHEA (Fig. 5H, I and S5E). We also inhibited FXR during L. sa and DHEA co-treatment (Fig. S5F) and demonstrated that FXR blockade ameliorated insulin resistance (Fig. S5G and H), the rise in serum hormone levels (Fig. S5I), estrous cycle disruption (Fig. S5J), and ovarian injury (Fig. S5K and L) caused by L. sa and DHEA.

To confirm the role of intestinal FXR activation in Neu5Ac-mediated exacerbation of PCOS, we treated intestine-specific Fxr knockout (Fxr△IE) and control floxed (Fxrfl/fl) mice with Neu5Ac under DHEA-induced PCOS conditions (Fig. 5J). Knockout efficiency was confirmed by qPCR (Fig. S6A). The results showed that Neu5Ac exacerbated DHEA-induced PCOS in Fxrfl/fl mice, whereas these exacerbating effects were abolished in Fxr△IE mice (Fig. 5K-M and S6B-E). Moreover, TUDCA treatment alleviated PCOS induced by co-treatment with Neu5Ac and DHEA in Fxrfl/fl mice. However, intestinal Fxr knockout significantly attenuated TUDCA-mediated protection against PCOS (Fig. 5N–Q and S5G–I). Altogether, these findings demonstrate that Neu5Ac- and L. sa-induced alterations in bile acid profiles exacerbate PCOS through FXR activation.

5. Increased FXR activation exacerbates PCOS by inhibiting IL-22 production.
We next investigated how FXR activation promotes DHEA-induced PCOS in mice. FXR activation has been recently associated with suppression of IL-22 release in the gut 18, and reduced IL-22 levels are negatively correlated with PCOS development 1. To this end, we measured IL-22 levels under various treatment conditions. Indeed, DHEA-treated mice exhibited decreased ileal mRNA expression of IL-22 and its downstream target Reg3β compared to control mice, and Neu5Ac treatment further exacerbated these reductions (Fig. 6A). Similarly, serum IL-22 levels were reduced in DHEA-treated mice and further declined following Neu5Ac administration (Fig. 6B). Consistently, L. sa treatment also intensified the DHEA-induced decrease in IL-22 (Fig. 6C and D). We confirmed that the Neu5Ac- and L. sa-mediated reduction in IL-22 is mediated by bile acid-regulated FXR activation, as inhibition of BSH or FXR inhibition alleviated the decline in IL-22 caused by Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment (Fig. 6E and F). Moreover, TUDCA treatment reversed the reduction in IL-22 levels induced by Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment in Fxrfl/fl mice, whereas this effect was abolished in Fxr△IE mice (Fig. 6G). We then administered recombinant murine IL-22 (rMuIL-22) to mice during Neu5Ac and DHEA exposure 11 (Fig. 6H). rMuIL-22 treatment alleviated insulin resistance in Neu5Ac- and DHEA-co-treated mice (Fig. 6I and S7A). Administration of rMuIL-22 also improved estrous cycle disruption under Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment (Fig. 6J). Additionally, rMuIL-22 ameliorated ovarian damage and normalized serum hormone levels in mice receiving Neu5Ac and DHEA (Fig. 6K, L and S7B). Since bile acid-mediated TGR5 activation regulates IL-22 production and is involved in PCOS pathogenesis 1, we investigated whether the TUDCA-mediated increase in IL-22 was regulated by TGR5 activation. To this end, TUDCA-treated mice were subjected to TGR5 inhibition using SBI-115 25,26. However, TGR5 inhibition by SBI-115 did not affect the TUDCA-mediated increase in IL-22 (Fig. S7D) or the alleviation of PCOS in mice (Fig. S7E–J). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that increased FXR activation exacerbates PCOS by suppressing IL-22 production.

6. IL-22 alleviates DHEA-induced PCOS by inhibiting ferroptosis through STAT3 activation.
Ferroptosis is closely implicated in the pathogenesis of PCOS, and IL-22 has been associated with potential anti-ferroptotic effects 5,11. To investigate whether IL-22 ameliorates PCOS by suppressing ferroptosis under Neu5Ac treatment, we first showed that DHEA-treated mice exhibited increased ovarian cell death compared to control mice, and this effect was further exacerbated by Neu5Ac or L. sa administration (Fig. 7A and S8A). However, treatment with Neu5Ac alone did not affect cell viability in vitro (Fig. S8B). Inhibition of FXR or treatment with rMuIL-22 attenuated ovarian cell death induced by co-treatment with Neu5Ac and DHEA (Fig. 7B and S8C). Moreover, DHEA treatment increased ovarian expression of PTGS2 and reduced GPX4 levels relative to controls, and these changes were amplified by Neu5Ac treatment (Fig. 7C). Importantly, rMuIL-22 treatment mitigated the DHEA- and Neu5Ac-induced upregulation of PTGS2 and downregulation of GPX4 in the ovary (Fig. 7D). Additionally, DHEA-treated mice displayed elevated oxidative stress, as evidenced by increased malondialdehyde (MDA) and decreased glutathione (GSH) levels, which were further aggravated by Neu5Ac and L. sa treatments (Fig. S8D and E). Similarly, DHEA increased ovarian Fe²⁺ levels compared to control mice, an effect further intensified by Neu5Ac and L. sa (Fig. S8F). In contrast, FXR inhibition or rMuIL-22 administration reduced ovarian oxidative stress and Fe²⁺ accumulation in Neu5Ac- and DHEA-co-treated mice (Fig. S8G and H).

To determine the extent to which the protective effect of IL-22 against PCOS is mediated by ferroptosis inhibition, we treated cells and mice with ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1), a specific ferroptosis inhibitor 5,11. In vitro, both rMuIL-22 and Fer-1 alleviated DHEA-induced cell death compared to control cells, and no additional benefit was observed with combined rMuIL-22 and Fer-1 treatment relative to either agent alone (Fig. 7E). Additionally, both rMuIL-22 and Fer-1 individually improved insulin resistance (Fig. S9A and B) and ameliorated estrous cycle disruption caused by Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment (Fig. S9C and D). Furthermore, both treatments attenuated ovarian damage and normalized serum hormone levels (Fig. 7F, G and S9E). However, the effects in mice receiving rMuIL-22 and Fer-1 together were comparable to those treated with either agent alone (Fig. 7F, G and S9A–E).

STAT3 is a downstream signaling target of IL-22 and has been reported to exert anti-ferroptotic effects 11. As expected, mice subjected to Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment exhibited reduced phosphorylated STAT3 (p-STAT3) levels compared to controls, and rMuIL-22 treatment reversed this suppression (Fig. 7H). Administration of Stattic, a selective STAT3 inhibitor 11, abolished the protective effects of rMuIL-22 against DHEA-induced cell death (Fig. 7I) and attenuated rMuIL-22-mediated downregulation of PTGS2 and upregulation of GPX4 (Fig. 7J). Likewise, Stattic treatment reversed the beneficial effects of rMuIL-22 on insulin resistance (Fig. 7K and S9F), estrous cycle disruption (Fig. S9G), ovarian injury (Fig. 7L and M), and serum hormone imbalances in the context of Neu5Ac and DHEA co-treatment (Fig. S9H). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that IL-22 alleviates DHEA-induced PCOS by inhibiting ferroptosis via STAT3 activation.
paper_content.methods:
Human participants
The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of China-Japan Union Hospital, Jilin University (2025101111). The 2003 Rotterdam criteria were used to distinguish patients with PCOS from healthy controls. A diagnosis of PCOS requires the presence of at least two of the following three features, as previously defined 1,7: (a) oligo- and/or anovulation; (b) clinical and/or biochemical evidence of hyperandrogenism; and (c) polycystic ovarian morphology. In addition, other potential etiologies—such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting tumors, and Cushing’s syndrome—were excluded through appropriate clinical evaluations. Moreover, all participants had not used antibiotics, probiotics, or hormonal medications in the past month and had not been pregnant or breastfeeding within the previous year. All PCOS patients were newly diagnosed and had not received any pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions for PCOS prior to enrollment. In Cohort 1, human serum and fecal samples were collected from 16 PCOS patients and 16 healthy controls at the China-Japan Union Hospital of Jilin University. The clinical characteristics of these participants are presented in Supplementary Table 1. In an independent validation cohort (Cohort 2), fecal samples were collected from 19 PCOS patients and 14 healthy controls at the same institution (clinical characteristics are provided in Supplementary Table 2) for measurement of fecal Neu5Ac levels. This study included only female participants, with sex determined by self-report. Written informed consent was obtained from all individuals prior to participation.

Animal and treatments
The animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Jilin University (SY2025120304). Female C57BL/6 mice at the prepubertal stage (21 days old) were obtained from Liaoning Changsheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Benxi, China) and housed under a 12-hour light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water at a temperature of 22.5 ± 2.5 °C and humidity of 50 ± 5% in a strictly controlled SPF environment. Villin Cre mice and Fxr-fl/fl mice were purchased from Cyagen. Intestinal-specific Fxr knockout (Fxr△IE) mice were generated by crossing 6–8-week-old villin Cre mice and Fxr-fl/fl mice. Villin Cre mice, Fxr-fl/fl mice and Fxr△IE mice were on a C57BL/6J genetic background.

To induce PCOS, prepubertal female mice were subcutaneously injected with DHEA (HY-14650, MCE) at a dose of 60 mg/kg body weight daily for 21 consecutive days 1. Mice in the control group received 200 μL of sesame oil via the same administration route. For Neu5Ac treatment, mice were fed a standard AIN93G diet and supplemented with 1% Neu5Ac (A0812, Sigma-Aldrich, MO, USA) in drinking water, along with oral gavage of 1 mg/200 μL Neu5Ac twice daily for 21 days 21. For antibiotic-mediated depletion of commensal microbes, mice received 1 g/L ampicillin (Cat# A5354, Sigma), neomycin (Cat# N6386, Sigma), and metronidazole (Cat# 16677, Sigma), and 0.5 g/L vancomycin (Cat# V2002, Sigma) in drinking water throughout the experimental period. For fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), recipient mice were treated with a cocktail of antibiotics (200 mg/kg body weight/day of ampicillin, neomycin, and metronidazole; 100 mg/kg body weight/day vancomycin) for 6 days, followed by a 1-day washout period with regular water, then subjected to FMT for 7 consecutive days, and maintained under standard conditions thereafter. For L. sa treatment, mice were pretreated with the same antibiotic regimen for 6 days, followed by a 1-day washout, and then orally administered L. sa (2 × 10⁸ CFUs per mouse) daily for 7 days, followed by continued treatment during the subsequent 21-day DHEA exposure period. For TUDCA treatment, mice were administered 30 mg/kg TUDCA (HY-19696, MCE) daily for 21 days 1. For TGR5 inhibition in the context of TUDCA treatment, mice were treated with TUDCA and either with or without SBI-115 (80 mg/kg/day, HY-111534, MCE) for 21 days 26. For BSH inhibition, mice were treated with caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE) (75 mg/kg/day, HY-N0274, MCE) for 21 days 24. For FXR inhibition, mice received Gly-β-MCA (50 mg/kg, HY-114392, MCE) daily for 21 days in combination with Neu5Ac or L. sa treatment 32. For IL-22 treatment, mice were injected with recombinant murine IL-22 (rMuIL-22, HY-P7079, MCE) at 1 mg/kg daily for 21 days 11. For ferroptosis inhibition, mice were treated with ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1, 10 mg/kg, HY-100579, MCE) daily, administered 2 hours prior to DHEA injection, for 21 days 11. For STAT3 inhibition, mice were treated with 10 mg/kg Stattic (HY-13818, MCE) daily for 21 days concurrently with Neu5Ac and DHEA administration 11.

Cell culture and treatments
KGN cells were obtained from the Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources (JCRB 1150) and cultured in F12 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, CA, USA) and 1% antibiotic-antimycotic solution (penicillin/streptomycin) at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. Cells were seeded into six-well plates and allowed to adhere overnight, after which the medium was replaced with antibiotic-free culture medium. For Neu5Ac treatment, cells were treated with Neu5Ac (0, 6.25, 12.5 and 25 mg/mL) for 24 h 28. For Fer-1 treatment, cells were pretreated with 1 μM Fer-1 with or without 0.1 μg/mL rMuIL-22 for 2 h, followed by incubation with DHEA (20 μM) for an additional 24 h 11. For STAT3 inhibition, cells were pretreated with 20 μM Stattic for 1 h, then exposed to rMuIL-22 (0.1 μg/mL) for 2 h, and subsequently treated with DHEA (20 μM) for 24 h 11.

Vaginal smears and estrous cycle determination
Vaginal smears and estrous cycle assessment were performed as previously described 36. Briefly, vaginal smears were collected daily from the 10th to the 19th day after the initiation of DHEA treatment. The stage of the estrous cycle was determined by microscopic examination of the predominant cell types in the smears following Shorr staining. The estrous cycle consists of four stages: proestrus (P), characterized by round, nucleated epithelial cells; estrus (E), marked by cornified squamous epithelial cells; metestrus (M), identified by a mixture of epithelial cells and leukocytes; and diestrus (D), dominated by leukocytes with scattered nucleated epithelial cells.

GTT and ITT assays
For the glucose tolerance test (GTT), mice were fasted for 12 hours on day 21 after the initiation of DHEA treatment. For the insulin tolerance test (ITT), a 4-hour fasting period was implemented. Baseline fasting blood glucose levels were measured prior to intraperitoneal injection of 2 mg/kg D-glucose (for GTT) or 1 IU/kg insulin (for ITT). Blood samples were then collected from the tail vein at 15, 30, 60, 90, and 120 min post-injection, and blood glucose concentrations were determined using the Roche Diagnostics Accu-Chek Performa blood glucose monitoring system.

Serum biochemical assays
Peripheral blood samples were processed using standardized pre-analytical procedures to ensure analyte stability. Blood samples were centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 5 min at 4 °C, after which serum was collected and combined with freshly obtained fecal samples; both were then aliquoted and immediately snap-frozen at −80 °C for batch analysis at a later time. Clinically relevant parameters were measured using previously established methods 1,7. Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone concentrations were determined by radioimmunoassay. Circulating levels of estradiol, testosterone, and androstenedione were quantified using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) on a Sciex Triple Quad 6500+ system. Glucose homeostasis was evaluated by calculating the homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) index using the standard formula: fasting blood glucose (mmol L−1) × fasting insulin (μIU mL−1) / 22.5. Mouse and human blood samples for ELISA were collected and centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C. Serum levels of IL-22 (88-7422-88, Thermo Scientific, USA), FGF15 (BES3006K, BIOESN, China), and FGF19 (EHFGF19, Thermo Scientific, USA) were measured according to the manufacturers’ instructions.

Histological analysis
Ovarian tissues for histological analysis were collected and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde. After dehydration and paraffin embedding, 5-μm-thick sections were prepared and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) as previously described 1,37. Histological changes were assessed using an optical microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan).

Immunofluorescence
Ovarian tissue sections were deparaffinized and rehydrated prior to apoptosis assessment using a terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) assay kit, following the manufacturer’s instructions (S7111, Sigma-Aldrich, USA). Apoptotic cells were labeled with fluorescence and visualized under a confocal microscope (Olympus, Japan). Fluorescent signals were quantified using ImageJ software 11.

Bacterial cultivation and growth analysis
Ligilactobacillus salivarius BNCC 138618 (L. salivarius) was cultivated in de Man, Rogosa, and Sharpe (MRS) broth (HB0384-1, Haibo, China) at 37 °C anaerobic conditions 13. To investigate the effect of Neu5Ac on bacterial proliferation, L. salivarius was cultured in M9 minimal medium (M9956, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) supplemented with either 10 mM Neu5Ac or an equimolar concentration of glucose as the sole carbon source. Bacterial growth was monitored by measuring optical density at 600 nm (OD₆₀₀) 21.

Cell viability analysis
Cells were treated as described above, and cell viability was determined using a commercial CCK-8 assay kit (Solarbio, Beijing, China) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Absorbance was measured after incubation of cells with the CCK-8 reagent in a 24-well plate 11.

GSH and MDA detections
GSH and MDA levels were determined using assay kits for GSH (A006-2, Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, China) and MDA (MAK085, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) following the manufacturers’ instructions.

Fe2+ level assay
Cellular Fe²⁺ levels were determined using a commercial kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions (E-BC-F101, Elabscience, China).

Neu5Ac level determination
Fecal and serum Neu5Ac levels were determined using the Sialic Acid Assay Kit (MAK314, Sigma-Aldrich, MO, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

DNA Extraction and 16S rRNA sequencing
Microbial genomic DNA was extracted from mouse fecal samples using the FastDNA® Spin Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. DNA quality and concentration were evaluated by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis and with a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). The V3–V4 hypervariable region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene was amplified using primers 338F and 806R on a GeneAmp® 9700 PCR system (ABI, USA). The PCR protocol included an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 27 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 45 s, and a final extension at 72 °C for 10 min. Each reaction was performed in triplicate. Amplified products were purified from 2% agarose gels using the AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit (Axygen Biosciences, USA) and quantified using a Quantus™ Fluorometer (Promega, USA). Equimolar amounts of purified amplicons were pooled and sequenced using paired-end technology on the Illumina MiSeq PE300 or NovaSeq PE250 platforms (Illumina, USA) at Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Sequences were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at a 97% sequence similarity threshold using UPARSE (v7.1), with chimeric sequences removed during the process. Taxonomic assignment was performed using the RDP Classifier (v2.2) against the 16S rRNA gene database with a minimum confidence threshold of 0.7. Microbial community structure was visualized by principal coordinate analysis (PCoA), and statistical differences were assessed using Adonis. Differentially abundant bacterial taxa were identified through linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe).

Untargeted metabolomics
Fecal metabolomics profiling was performed using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Briefly, serum samples were extracted with 400 µL of a methanol:water (4:1, v/v) solution containing 0.02 mg/mL L-2-chlorophenylalanine as the internal standard. The mixture was incubated at –20 °C for 30 minutes and then homogenized using a high-throughput tissue homogenizer (Wonbio-96c, Shanghai Wanbo Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) at 50 Hz for 6 minutes. This was followed by ultrasonication at 40 kHz for 30 minutes at 5 °C. Subsequently, the samples were maintained at –20 °C for an additional 30 minutes to induce protein precipitation. After centrifugation at 13,000×g at 4 °C for 15 minutes, the supernatant was carefully transferred into sample vials for LC-MS/MS analysis. Chromatographic conditions: A 2 μL sample was separated on an HSS T3 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm i.d., 1.8 µm) and then introduced into the mass spectrometer. The mobile phases consisted of 0.1% formic acid in water:acetonitrile (95:5, v/v) and 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile:isopropanol:water (47.5:47.5:5, v/v). MS conditions: Mass spectrometric data were acquired using a Thermo UHPLC-Q Exactive mass spectrometer equipped with an electrospray ionization (ESI) source operating in both positive and negative ion modes. Following mass spectrometry, raw LC-MS data were preprocessed using Progenesis QI software (Waters Corporation, Milford, USA). Variance analysis was performed on the matrix file after data preprocessing. Principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were conducted using the R package ropls (Version 1.6.2). A seven-cycle interactive validation was applied to assess model stability. Additionally, Student’s t-test and fold-change analysis were performed. Significantly different metabolites were selected based on the variable importance in the projection (VIP) values derived from the OPLS-DA model and the p-values from Student’s t-tests. Metabolites with VIP > 1 and p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Differential metabolites between groups were summarized and mapped to biochemical pathways through metabolic enrichment and pathway analysis via database searching (KEGG, http://www.genome.jp/kegg/). Data analysis was carried out using the free online platform MajorBio Cloud Platform (cloud.majorbio.com).

BSH Activity Assay
Ileal contents and fecal samples (50 mg each) were suspended in 250 μL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4) and homogenized by vortexing for 1 min. Bacterial lysis was achieved through sonication on ice (90 s total duration with a 30 s interval). After centrifugation (15,000 × g, 30 min, 4 °C), the supernatant was collected. Protein concentration was determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) with bovine serum albumin (BSA) as the standard, following the manufacturer’s protocol. The original protein solution was then diluted with PBS to a final working concentration of 2 mg/mL. BSH activity was measured by quantifying the enzymatic conversion of deuterium-labeled taurochenodeoxycholic acid (d4-TCDCA) to deuterium-labeled chenodeoxycholic acid (d4-CDCA). The reaction mixture (200 μL) consisted of 3 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.2), 0.1 mM d4-TCDCA, and 0.1 mg/mL of the diluted protein solution. Following incubation at 37 °C for 20 min, reactions were terminated by immediate freezing in dry ice. Methanol (100 μL) was added, followed by vortex mixing for 5 min and centrifugation (15,000 × g, 20 min, 4 °C). The resulting supernatant was analyzed by UPLC-TQMS (Waters, Milford, MA, USA) to quantify d4-CDCA levels, based on which BSH activity was calculated 19.

Bile acid analysis
Bile acid composition was analyzed using an established protocol 13. Quantification of bile acids in murine ileal content and human fecal samples was performed using an Agilent 1290 Infinity Liquid Chromatography system coupled to an Agilent 6470 triple quadrupole mass spectrometer. The method included a comprehensive panel of deuterated internal standards covering both conjugated and unconjugated bile acid species: cholic acid (CA), chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), deoxycholic acid (DCA), lithocholic acid (LCA), ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), and their glycine- and taurine-conjugated forms (GCA, GCDCA, GDCA, GLCA, GUDCA, TCA, TCDCA, TDCA, TLCA, TUDCA). Detection was conducted in negative electrospray ionization mode with multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). Instrument control and data acquisition were carried out using Agilent MassHunter software (B.08.00).

RNA extraction and qPCR
Total RNA was extracted using an RNA extraction kit (K0732, Thermo Scientific, USA). Briefly, cells were lysed with 1 mL of TRIzol reagent and subsequently subjected to phase separation using chloroform, followed by RNA precipitation with isopropanol and washing with 75% ethanol under RNase-free conditions. Following RNA extraction, complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized using TransStart Tip Green qPCR SuperMix (TransGen Biotech, Beijing, China). Quantitative RT–PCR was performed using gene-specific primers and FastStart Universal SYBR Green Master Mix (ROX) (Roche, Basel, Switzerland) on a StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). The primers used in this study were provided in Supplementary Table 3. The thermal cycling conditions were as follows: 52 °C for 2 min, 95 °C for 10 min, followed by 45 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s and 60 °C for 1 min 37,38. The 16S rRNA or GAPDH gene was used as the internal reference control. Relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method normalized to the control group.

Western blotting
Ovarian tissues or cultured cells were collected and subjected to protein extraction using a commercially available kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Total protein concentration was determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Target proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) according to their molecular weights. The proteins were then transferred onto 0.45 μm PVDF membranes and blocked with 5% skim milk for 3 hours at room temperature. Subsequently, the following primary antibodies were applied for overnight incubation at 4 °C: PTGS2 (1:1000, AF7003, Affinity Biosciences, USA), GPX4 (1:1000, AF7003, Affinity Biosciences, USA), STAT3 (1:1000, AF6294, Affinity Biosciences, USA), p-STAT3 (1:1000, AF3293, Affinity Biosciences, USA), and β-actin (1:1000, AF7018, Affinity Biosciences, USA). Following three 20-minute washes with PBST to remove unbound antibodies, the membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:2000, goat anti-rabbit or rabbit anti-mouse IgG) for 2 hours at room temperature. After an additional three PBST washes, protein expression levels were visualized using an ECL Plus Western Blotting Detection System (Tanon 4500, Shanghai, China).

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0 (San Diego, CA, USA). No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size for animal experiments or in vitro studies; however, the sample sizes used in this study are consistent with those reported in previously published work 1,7. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or boxplots, where the center line represents the median, the box spans the interquartile range (25th to 75th percentiles), and the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values. Normality of data distribution was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. The Mann–Whitney U test (non-parametric) and two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (parametric) were used to evaluate significant differences between two groups. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was applied. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Sidak’s multiple-comparisons correction was used to analyze the GTT and ITT assays. For these assays, p values with a bracket line connecting two groups refer to the whole curves and p values on top of individual datapoints refer only to indicated time point. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All experiments were performed at least three independent experiments, with similar results across replicates.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, the authors report the identification of N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) as a novel biomarker for
polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) through non-targeted metabolomics of a clinical cohort. They further propose that
Neu5Ac aggravates PCOS mainly by increasing the abundance of Lactobacillus salivarius (L.sa) and its bile-salt-hydrolase
(BSH) activity, leading to a reduction in the conjugated bile acid TCDCA. The decrease in TCDCA, in turn, exacerbates
PCOS via FXR–IL-22 axis. While the discovery of Neu5Ac is interesting, the clinical evidence is preliminary and the
mechanistic elaboration remains superficial. Major revisions are required.
1. Sample size is too small. The authors should expand the discovery cohort and, ideally, validate the findings in an
independent cohort. Do public metabolomic datasets show a similar association between Neu5Ac and PCOS?
2. Which organ/tissue is the primary source of Neu5Ac? What are the concentrations of Neu5Ac in peripheral blood and the
ovarian micro-environment? Does Neu5Ac exert any direct effect on ovarian cells (granulosa/theca cells or oocytes)?
3. Is serum or follicular-fluid Neu5Ac level correlated with PCOS severity, phenotype (hyper-androgenic vs. non-hyper-
androgenic), BMI, insulin resistance indices, or ovulatory dysfunction?
4. In PCOS patients, is Neu5Ac abundance correlated with L.sa relative abundance? Can Neu5Ac, in vitro, directly promote
the growth of L.sa or other BSH-expressing taxa?
5. In PCOS patients, does Neu5Ac correlate with the overall bile-acid profile, especially with FXR-antagonistic conjugated
bile acids?
6. The bile-acid pool composition differs markedly between humans and rodents; glycine-conjugated species (GUDCA,
GDCA) are abundant in humans and are potent FXR/TGR5 modulators. The authors should quantify these human-relevant
bile acids in their clinical samples rather than relying solely on murine data.
7. Bile acids usually regulate FXR at the transcriptional-activity level, not by altering FXR protein abundance. The
observation that DHEA, Neu5Ac and L.sa increase FXR protein levels is counter-intuitive. What is the underlying molecular
mechanism (stabilization of FXR protein? decreased proteasomal degradation? transcriptional up-regulation)?
8. Genetic loss-of-function studies are indispensable. Does Neu5Ac-dependent exacerbation of PCOS phenotypes
disappear in intestinal-specific FXR-knockout mice (FXRΔint)?
9. GDCA–TGR5–IL-22 axis is reported to involve in PCOS pathogenesis. TCDCA is not only an FXR antagonist but also a
TGR5 agonist. Is the suppression of IL-22 by Neu5Ac mediated via TGR5, FXR, or both?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The role of the gut microbiota in PCOS progression remains unclear. Although the gut microbiome differs in individuals with
PCOS, these differences alone do not establish a causal role in disease development. Drug treatments are known to alter
the gut microbiota, further complicating interpretation and weakening arguments for causation. A major limitation of both
preclinical and clinical studies is the lack of in-depth mechanistic investigation into how gut microbiota might interact with
androgen excess. While elevated androgens may contribute to dysbiosis, evidence that gut microbiota alterations can drive
PCOS pathophysiology is scarce, if not entirely absent. For this reason, the statement that “the gut microbiota has been
recognized as an important modulator of PCOS pathogenesis” overstates the current evidence base.
That said, I appreciate the authors’ ambitious approach in this manuscript, particularly their efforts to dissect mechanistic
underpinnings. The authors present evidence for an intriguing pathway in which Ligilactobacillus influences Neu5Ac
availability, thereby altering bile acid metabolism. This shift activates intestinal FXR signaling, ultimately reducing IL-22
production. Diminished circulating IL-22 may have systemic consequences, including impaired ovarian function. These
findings suggest a promising therapeutic opportunity targeting the bile acid–FXR–IL-22 axis for the treatment of PCOS.
Suggestions for revision.
The introduction is too long.
Refrain to use the term healthy controls, healthy group or healthy individuals. They may have other conditions although not
PCOS. Controls is an appropriate term.
Results
Fig. 1C. Present all differently expressed metabolites as supplemental material.
Fig 1G-M. Neu5Ac exposure alone does not have an effect in mice with a normal gut flora. How can this be explained? Why
is the combination with DHEA necessary for an effect?
Do not cut the axes in graphs as this is misleading.
Double-check the statistics in Fig 2B, is this really a significant difference? The curves are basically on top of each other.
Check this statement on line 184: We next quantified different Ligilactobacillus species using qPCR and found that
Ligilactobacillus salivarius (L. sa), but not L. reuteri or L. rhamnosus, was elevated in Neu5Ac- and N-FMT-treated mice, as
well as in PCOS patients (Fig. 4F–H and S2D–F). I belive it should be that Ligilactobacillus salivarius was elevated in
Neu5Ac+DHEA exposed mice. Moreover, L. reuteri and L. rhamnosus, seems to be elevated in Neu5Ac+DHEA and N-FMT-
treated mice (S2D-E).
Check labelling of groups in Fig 6B.
Statistics.
Glucose curves following ITT and GTT should be analyzed using repeated measurement ANOVA with appropriate
correction for multiple groups.
Include the statistics used in all graphs in the figure legend. For example, the statistics used in 1D is missing.
Material and methods
Describe the clinical cohort in more detail. Include, age, weight, BMI, androgen levels, LH, FSH, FG-score, ovarian
morphology, insulin and glucose levels etc.
Testosterone should not be measured by ELISA or RIA since they are unspecific. Tanden mass spectrometry should be
used for accurate measurements of androgens in humans and mice.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Thank you for your letter and for the reviewers’ comments concerning our manuscript entitled
“Sialic acid exacerbates polycystic ovary syndrome in mice by modulating the bile acid–FXR–
IL-22–ferroptosis axis” (NCOMMS-25-82445). These comments are all valuable and very helpful
for revising and improving our paper, as well as the important guiding significance to our researches.
We have addressed all the concerns raised by reviews. Below are our responses to the editors' and
reviewers' comments.
In order to facilitate the review, the blue font indicates reviewer’s comments, the black font indicates
the responses to reviewers, and the red font indicates the modification in the revised manuscript.
The responds to the reviewer’s comments are as follows:
Point-by-point response.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, the authors report the identification of N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) as a
novel biomarker for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) through non-targeted metabolomics of a
clinical cohort. They further propose that Neu5Ac aggravates PCOS mainly by increasing the
abundance of Lactobacillus salivarius (L.sa) and its bile-salt-hydrolase (BSH) activity, leading to a
reduction in the conjugated bile acid TCDCA. The decrease in TCDCA, in turn, exacerbates PCOS
via FXR–IL-22 axis. While the discovery of Neu5Ac is interesting, the clinical evidence is
preliminary and the mechanistic elaboration remains superficial. Major revisions are required.
Comment 1: Sample size is too small. The authors should expand the discovery cohort and, ideally,
validate the findings in an independent cohort. Do public metabolomic datasets show a similar
association between Neu5Ac and PCOS?
Response 1: We gratefully acknowledge the reviewer for the valuable time spent providing
constructive comments. We have measured fecal Neu5Ac levels in an independent cohort and
observed consistent results. Additionally, we analyzed the association between Neu5Ac and PCOS
using published metabolic datasets. However, most studies have primarily focused on serum
metabolic alterations in PCOS, with limited attention paid to fecal metabolic profiles. To date, no
studies have reported an association between fecal Neu5Ac levels and PCOS. We sincerely thank
the reviewer once again.
Line 81-83: This finding was replicated in an independent cohort consisting of 19 PCOS patients
and 14 control individuals (Fig. 1E and Supplementary table 3).
Fig. 1. Neu5Ac exacerbates DHEA-induced PCOS in a gut microbiota-dependent manner in

Neu5Ac in peripheral blood and the ovarian micro-environment? Does Neu5Ac exert any direct
effect on ovarian cells (granulosa/theca cells or oocytes)?
Response 2: We sincerely appreciate your professional suggestions. Studies have reported that
Neu5Ac is released from the mucosa under conditions of gut dysbiosis by bacteria expressing
sialidase (e.g., Bacteroides species, which are increased in PCOS) and by host macrophages;
however, these findings require further validation within the context of PCOS pathogenesis, and we
have discussed this limitation. We also measured circulating Neu5Ac concentrations and evaluated
the effects of Neu5Ac on ovarian cells. Thank you again for your valuable comments.

rule out the possibility that host cells in a diseased state may drive the release of Neu5Ac 27.

Limitations of the study
Although we have elucidated the crucial roles of Neu5Ac-mediated bile acid metabolism and FXR
activation in the pathogenesis of PCOS, the specific bacterial sources or host tissues responsible for
Neu5Ac production remain unclear. The mechanisms underlying the interaction between gut
microbiota and hormonal fluctuations in PCOS, as well as how this process is regulated by Neu5Ac,
are still unknown. Moreover, the contribution of metabolic alterations beyond bile acid
dysregulation to Neu5Ac-mediated PCOS progression remains to be determined. Future studies
should investigate the precise regulatory mechanisms by which Neu5Ac modulates the gut
microbiota and assess the therapeutic potential of targeting this pathway in PCOS.

with particular focus on FXR-antagonistic conjugated bile acids. We appreciate your feedback once

glycine-conjugated species (GUDCA, GDCA) are abundant in humans and are potent FXR/TGR5
modulators. The authors should quantify these human-relevant bile acids in their clinical samples
rather than relying solely on murine data.
Response 6: Thanks so much for your valuable comments. We have detected bile acid profiles in
PCOS patients and healthy individuals. Thanks again.

detected (Fig. 4C-D).
Fig. 4. Ligilactobacillus expansion promotes PCOS by altering bile acid profiles via bile salt
hydrolase. (C and D) Fecal bile acid profiles in PCOS patients and controls (n = 16).
Comment 7: Bile acids usually regulate FXR at the transcriptional-activity level, not by altering
FXR protein abundance. The observation that DHEA, Neu5Ac and L.sa increase FXR protein levels
is counter-intuitive. What is the underlying molecular mechanism (stabilization of FXR protein?
decreased proteasomal degradation? transcriptional up-regulation)?
Response 7: We sincerely thank you for your valuable and constructive suggestions. We fully agree
with the reviewer's viewpoint that bile acids typically regulate FXR at the transcriptional level.
However, studies have also reported that bile acids can modulate FXR protein levels (Science. 2025.
PMID: 40179178; Nat Commun. 2019. PMID: 31672964). In this study, we observed that DHEA,
Neu5Ac, and L. sa increase both the transcriptional and protein levels of FXR. This effect may result
from transcriptional upregulation mediated by bile acid metabolism. However, we are currently
unable to confirm the specific molecular mechanisms involved, and cannot exclude other potential
pathways—such as FXR protein stabilization, reduced proteasomal degradation (as suggested by
the reviewer), or bile acid-independent mechanisms. To avoid misinterpretation, we have removed
the data related to FXR protein levels and plan to investigate this question in greater depth in future
studies. We appreciate your constructive feedback once again.
Comment 8: Genetic loss-of-function studies are indispensable. Does Neu5Ac-dependent
exacerbation of PCOS phenotypes disappear in intestinal-specific FXR-knockout mice (FXRΔint)?
Response 8: We gratefully appreciate for your valuable comments. We have supplemented genetic
loss-of-function studies by using intestinal epithelial-specific FXR-knockout mice (FxrΔIE), and
found that Neu5Ac-mediated exacerbation on PCOS was eliminated in FxrΔIE mice. Thanks again.
Line 215-219: To confirm the role of intestinal FXR activation in Neu5Ac-mediated exacerbation
of PCOS, we treated intestine-specific Fxr knockout (Fxr△IE) and control floxed (Fxrfl/fl) mice with
Neu5Ac under DHEA-induced PCOS conditions (Fig. 5J). Knockout efficiency was confirmed by
qPCR (Fig. S6A). The results showed that Neu5Ac exacerbated DHEA-induced PCOS in Fxrfl/fl
mice, whereas these exacerbating effects were abolished in Fxr△IE mice (Fig. 5K-M and S6B-E).
Fig. 5. Alterations in bile acid profile aggravate PCOS by activating FXR. (J) Schematic
diagram illustrating the experimental design of Neu5Ac treatment in Fxrfl/fl and intestine-specific
Fxr knockout (Fxr△IE) mice. (K) GTT and ITT assays in the different treatment groups (n = 5). *p
< 0.05 and ***p < 0.001 indicate significant differences between the Neu5Ac + DHEA + Fxrfl/fl
group and the DHEA + Fxrfl/fl group; #p < 0.05, ##p < 0.01, and ###p < 0.001 indicate significant
differences between the Neu5Ac + DHEA + Fxr△IE group and the Neu5Ac + DHEA + Fxrfl/fl group.

Quantification of cystic follicles and corpora lutea (n = 5).
Comment 9: GDCA–TGR5–IL-22 axis is reported to involve in PCOS pathogenesis. TCDCA is
not only an FXR antagonist but also a TGR5 agonist. Is the suppression of IL-22 by Neu5Ac
mediated via TGR5, FXR, or both?
Response 9: We gratefully appreciate your professional advice. We fully agree with the reviewer's
observation that conjugated bile acids may influence the PCOS process not only through FXR
inhibition but also via activation of the TGR5-IL-22 signaling pathway. However, our findings
indicate that Neu5Ac-mediated exacerbation of PCOS is primarily driven by FXR dysregulation.
First, the detrimental effects of Neu5Ac were alleviated by treatment with the FXR antagonist Gly-
β-MCA. Second, Neu5Ac-mediated exacerbation of PCOS was abolished in FxrΔIE mice.
Furthermore, in response to the reviewers' suggestions, we analyzed human bile acid profiles and
found that Neu5Ac levels were predominantly associated with reduced concentrations of TUDCA—
a bile acid with weak TGR5 activation potential. Notably, TUDCA supplementation ameliorated
Neu5Ac-induced worsening of PCOS in mice, and this beneficial effect persisted in the presence of

Line 19-67: Introduction
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent endocrine disorder characterized by ovarian
dysfunction and insulin resistance, adversely affecting ovarian health and female reproductive
function. In PCOS, the ovary exhibits increased inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death,
including ferroptosis. Deficiency of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a key regulator of redox
homeostasis during ferroptosis, exacerbates ferroptosis and contributes to endometrial epithelial
fibrosis in PCOS. Additionally, the gut microbiota has been implicated in PCOS pathogenesis. For
instance, patients with PCOS exhibit significant gut dysbiosis, particularly elevated levels of fecal
Bacteroides vulgatus (B. vulgatus), and administration of B. vulgatus induces PCOS-like symptoms
in mice. Modulation of the gut microbiota through inulin and tempol treatment alleviates PCOS and
associated metabolic disturbances. However, the roles of specific microbial species in PCOS
pathogenesis remains poorly understood.
Gut microbiota-derived metabolites are key mediators that regulate the crosstalk between the
intestinal microbiota and the host. For example, patients with PCOS exhibit altered bile acid profiles,
particularly increased levels of non-conjugated bile acids and reduced levels of conjugated bile acids
such as glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCA) and tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA). Treatment of
mice with GDCA and TUDCA ameliorates PCOS by increasing interleukin-22 (IL-22) levels, which
may be attributed to enhanced IL-22 production and subsequent activation of signal transducer and
activator of transcription 3 (STAT3). Conjugated bile acids can be converted into non-conjugated
forms by gut microbiota through bile salt hydrolase (BSH) activity, and bacterial genera enriched in
PCOS patients—such as Bacteroides and Lactobacillus—exhibit high BSH expression. Notably,
conjugated bile acids, including TUDCA, and GDCA, typically act as antagonists of farnesoid X
receptor (FXR). Enhanced intestinal FXR activation promotes the development of metabolic
disorders through multiple mechanisms, such as promoting ceramide synthesis. Additionally, gut-
specific FXR activation reduces IL-22 levels by promoting intestinal epithelial ferroptosis and lipid
peroxide accumulation. Inhibition of BSH activity or intestinal FXR signaling exerts beneficial
effects against metabolic syndrome and pathological cell death.
Although gut microbiota-derived metabolites directly influence metabolic health and the
development of PCOS, little is known about how microbial metabolism reciprocally affects gut
homeostasis. For example, alterations in the gut microbiota and the presence of gut inflammation
increase the release of free N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac, also known as sialic acid), a 9-carbon
monosaccharide located on the outer layer of the intestinal mucosa. This release exacerbates gut
dysbiosis, promotes intestinal inflammation, and contributes to extraintestinal diseases such as
mastitis. Bacteroides efficiently produces free sialic acid via its sialidase enzyme but lacks the
capacity to utilize sialic acid for growth. In contrast, commensal Lactobacillus and opportunistic
pathobionts such as Escherichia/Shigella can exploit sialic acid as a carbon source to support their
proliferation in the gut, thereby influencing disease outcomes. However, it remains unclear whether
Bacteroides-derived sialic acid facilitates the expansion of Lactobacillus and Escherichia/Shigella
and thereby promotes the development of PCOS.
In this study, we found that patients with PCOS exhibited elevated fecal Neu5Ac levels, which
exacerbated PCOS in a gut microbiota-dependent manner. Specifically, Neu5Ac treatment promoted
the expansion of the gut Ligilactobacillus salivarius (L. sa) and increased BSH activity, thereby
reducing levels of the conjugated bile acid TUDCA, enhancing intestinal FXR activation, and
suppressing IL-22 release. This cascade ultimately aggravates PCOS by promoting ovarian
ferroptosis through modulation of STAT3 signaling. These findings indicate that sialic acid
promotes gut dysbiosis and FXR activation, thereby exacerbating PCOS outcomes.

Serum biochemical assays
Peripheral blood samples were processed using standardized pre-analytical procedures to ensure
analyte stability. Blood samples were centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 5 min at 4 °C, after which serum
was collected and combined with freshly obtained fecal samples; both were then aliquoted and
immediately snap-frozen at −80 °C for batch analysis at a later time. Clinically relevant parameters
were measured using previously established methods. Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating
hormone concentrations were determined by radioimmunoassay. Circulating levels of estradiol,
testosterone, and androstenedione were quantified using liquid chromatography–tandem mass
spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) on a Sciex Triple Quad 6500+ system. Glucose homeostasis was
evaluated by calculating the homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) index
using the standard formula: fasting blood glucose (mmol L−1) × fasting insulin (μIU mL−1) / 22.5.
